lines.translit: iri^ki kug-kug-ga-am3 e-ne ba-am3-me-en-ze2-en kur dilmun^ki kug-ga-am3

i18n.en: The city is pure — those who are you — the land of Dilmun is pure.

lines.commentary:
The composition opens with the canonical Sumerian Dilmun-paradise formula: the toponym *kur dilmun^ki* is qualified by the adjective *kug* 'pure / holy / shining' and (in following lines) by its near-synonyms *sikil* 'pure / virginal' and *dadag* 'bright'. *kur dilmun* — literally 'the (mountain-)land Dilmun' — is the archaeologically-attested Bahrain-archipelago and adjacent eastern-Arabian-Gulf region, attested in third-millennium BCE trade-tablets as an emporium for the Indus-Gulf-Mesopotamia network. The literary tradition makes Dilmun the **eastern paradise-land**, and this composition is the most-developed Sumerian source for that tradition (Kramer 'Dilmun, the Land of the Living' *BASOR* 96 (1944); Kramer 'Dilmun: Quest for Paradise' *Antiquity* 37 (1963); Alster *Dilmun, the Cradle of Civilization* 1983; D. T. Potts *The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity* 1990; Crawford *Dilmun and Its Gulf Neighbours* 1998).

The Dilmun-paradise tradition pairs cross-corpus with the Hebrew Gen 2:8 *gan b-Eden mi-qedem* 'a garden in Eden, in the east' (see Hebrew central entry `gan-be-eden`). The comparative-mythology link — the **eastern-paradise locus** as a structural feature of both Sumerian and Hebrew cosmography — is documented as named scholarship: Albright 'The Mouth of the Rivers' *AJSL* 35 (1919); Heidel *The Babylonian Genesis* 1942; Cassuto *From Adam to Noah* 1961; Jacobsen *The Treasures of Darkness* 1976; Wenham *Genesis 1-15* WBC 1987; Hallo *Origins* 1996; Sarna *Genesis* JPS Commentary 1989. The link is **comparative-mythology and shared cosmographic motif**, not philological cognation (Sumerian and Hebrew belong to unrelated language-families; *Dilmun* is not etymologically related to *Eden*). The popular-fringe interpretations of Dilmun as a spaceport (Sitchin) or as an Anunnaki-installation are not engaged here; the central entry `dilmun-eastern-paradise-cross-corpus` documents the disavowals.

lines.translit: kur dilmun^ki sikil-am3 kur dilmun^ki dadag-ga-am3

i18n.en: The land of Dilmun is pure; the land of Dilmun is bright.
When alone, he lay down in Dilmun —
the place where Enki lay down with his spouse —
that place is pure, that place is bright.
When alone, he lay down in Dilmun —
the place where Enki lay down with Ninsikila —
that place is pure, that place is bright.
In Dilmun the raven was uttering no cry,

lines.commentary:
Lines 11-28 are the famous **paradise-by-negation** rhetorical sequence: Dilmun is described not by what it has but by what it lacks. The raven utters no cry; the predator does not predate; the eye-sick one does not say 'I am sick'; the old woman does not say 'I am old'; the herald does not patrol the border; the singer raises no lament. The rhetorical figure defines paradise by enumerated negations of ordinary-world phenomena — illness, predation, aging, social-discord, lament. The Sumerian construction repeats the negative verbal-prefix *nu-* / *na-* across the sequence to mark each absence; the cumulative effect is a paradise whose substance is **the absence of the conditions of ordinary life**.

The figure is cross-corpus comparative-mythology shared with several Hebrew and wider-ANE paradise-traditions. **Isaiah 11:6-9** — the *ve-gar ze'ev im-keves* 'the wolf shall dwell with the lamb' messianic peaceable-kingdom — deploys the **no-predation** sub-pattern directly. **Isaiah 65:25** repeats the wolf-and-lamb image in a parallel eschatological-paradise frame. **Revelation 21:4** *ouk estai eti thanatos oude penthos* 'there shall be no more death, neither sorrow' deploys the **no-illness/no-lament** sub-pattern. **Genesis 2-3** carries the same paradise-by-implicit-negation: in Eden death does not occur until the disruption of Gen 3, and the absence-of-death is part of the garden's diagnostic state. **Hesiod *Works and Days* 109-126** describes the Golden Age in parallel-negative terms (no toil, no aging, no death-as-experienced-evil).

Named scholarship: Kramer 1944 *BASOR* 96 (the foundational comparative observation); Alster *Dilmun, the Cradle of Civilization* 1983; Black-Cunningham-Robson-Zolyomi 2004; Wenham *Genesis 1-15* WBC 1987 on the Edenic paradise-by-absence; Westermann *Genesis 1-11* BKAT on the comparative-mythology context; Sarna *Genesis* JPS 1989; on Isaiah 11: J. D. W. Watts *Isaiah 1-33* WBC 1985; on the wider ANE paradise-traditions: M. Stol 'Old Babylonian Cattle' BSA 8 (1995) on the predator-and-prey topos in Mesopotamian wisdom-literature. The pattern is a **structural-comparative-mythology** observation across independent traditions converging on the diagnostic 'paradise = absence of disruption'; no etymological-genealogical claim is made between the Sumerian and the Hebrew or NT material. See central entry `paradise-by-negation-no-predation-no-illness-no-aging-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: the francolin uttered no francolin-cry,
the lion did not strike with the head;
the wolf was not snatching lambs,
the dog had not learned to make kids crouch,
the pig had not learned to devour grain.
When a widow had spread malt on the roof,
the birds of heaven were not devouring that malt above.
The dove was not turning its head with it.
The eye-sick one was not saying, 'I am eye-sick.'
The headache-sufferer was not saying, 'I am sick with a headache.'
Its old woman was not saying, 'I am an old woman.'
Its old man was not saying, 'I am an old man.'
No unwashed maiden was made conspicuous in the city.
The man crossing the river was uttering no cry of distress at night.
The herald did not patrol his border-district.
The singer was not uttering a lament.
At the edge of the city, no wailing was being uttered.
Ninsikila spoke to her father Enki, saying:

'[A city without field,] without meadow, [without furrow] —'
[3 lines missing.]
[3 lines missing.] '[Utu, standing in heaven] —'
'from the breast of his stepping out at the Ezen-temple —'
'from the summit-shrine, splendor of Nanna —'

lines.translit: [ka a ki-a DU.DU-ta a dug3 ki-ta … DU]

i18n.en: 'from the mouth where the water runs out of the earth — sweet water coming forth from the earth ...'
'into your great basin let the water rise up.'
'May your city drink water of abundance through that.'
'May Dilmun drink water of <abundance> through that.'

lines.translit: pu2 a sis-a-zu pu2 a dug3-ga ḫe2-em

i18n.en: 'May your wells of bitter water become wells of sweet water.'
'May your city become a storehouse-quay of the Land.'
'May Dilmun become a store<house>-quay of the Land.'
Now, Utu of this day —

lines.commentary:
Lines 40-62 narrate the sun-god Utu's bringing-up of sweet water from below to irrigate Dilmun. The Sumerian *ka a ki-a DU.DU-ta a dug3 ki-ta* (43, 54) — 'from the mouth where the water runs out of the earth, sweet water from the earth' — is the diagnostic image: water rises from a subterranean source through a *ka* 'mouth' / aperture and is delivered into the *ĝiri3-ma-an gal* 'great basin' of the land. Utu's role here is the celestial-and-cosmic agent who effects the water-from-below — paralleling his more familiar function as the celestial sun and divine-judge (see central entry `utu-shamash-sun-god-justice-divinity-cross-corpus`).

The motif pairs cross-corpus with **Gen 2:6** *ve-ed ya'aleh min ha-aretz ve-hishqah et kol pnei ha-adamah* — 'and a mist (or watercourse) used to go up from the earth and water the whole face of the ground'. Both texts deploy the same structural image: **water rises from below to irrigate the paradisal land**, and the irrigation precedes (or grounds) the larger creation-or-paradise narrative. The Hebrew *ed* is itself a Sumero-Akkadian loanword (*id* / *edû* 'watercourse / spring-flood'; Speiser *Genesis* AB 1964; Westermann *Genesis 1-11* BKAT; Sarna *Genesis* JPS 1989), which suggests philological as well as motif-level Mesopotamian influence on the Hebrew Eden-prelude.

Named scholarship: Kramer 1944 *BASOR* 96; Hallo *Origins* 1996 on Dilmun-Eden cross-corpus; Westermann *Genesis 1-11* BKAT on Gen 2:6; Cassuto *From Adam to Noah* 1961 on the *ed*; Speiser *Genesis* AB 1964 on the Mesopotamian loanword; Wenham *Genesis 1-15* WBC 1987; on the wider Mesopotamian water-cosmology: Horowitz *Mesopotamian Cosmic Geography* 1998. The cross-corpus motif is documented as a **structural-cosmographic-parallel** (water-from-below as paradisal-irrigation); no claim is advanced beyond what named comparative scholarship supports. See central entry `water-from-below-irrigates-paradise-sumerian-hebrew-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: Utu, standing in heaven,
from the breast of his stepping out at the Ezen-temple,
from the summit-shrine, splendor of Nanna,

lines.translit: ka a ki-a DU.DU-ta a dug3 ki-ta mu-na-ra-DU

i18n.en: from the mouth where the water runs out of the earth — sweet water came forth from the earth for her.
Into her great [basin] the water rose up.
Her city drank water of abundance through it.
Dilmun drank water of <abundance> through it.

lines.translit: pu2 a sis-a-ni pu2> a dug3-ga na-nam

i18n.en: Her wells of bitter water became indeed wells of sweet water.
Her field, her meadow, her furrow brought forth grain for her.
Her city became indeed a storehouse-quay of the Land.
Dilmun became indeed a storehouse-quay of the Land.
Now, Utu of this day — so it was indeed.

lines.translit: dili-ni ( TAR) ĝeštug2-ge tuku-a ^dnin-tur5 ama kalam-ma-še3

i18n.en: She, the wise alone, to Nintur the mother of the Land —

lines.commentary: *Nintur* (the Lady of birth) is here named as *ama kalam-ma* 'mother of the Land' — one of the standard cult-epithets of the Sumerian birth-goddess. The text uses Nintur, Damgalnuna, and Ninhursag interchangeably as names of the same goddess; see central entry `nintur-nintud-ninhursaga-birth-goddess-epithet-cluster-cross-corpus` for the epithet-cluster scholarship.

i18n.en: Enki, the wise one, to Nintur the mother of the Land —
his penis he dug into the embankment for her.
His penis he sank into the reeds for her.
His penis he raised forth majestically from there.
He called out: 'In the marsh let no man seize me!'
Enki called out:
'By the life of heaven, I swear it!'

lines.commentary: The single-form oath *zi an-na* 'life of heaven' is the simplified variant of the standard Mesopotamian dual oath-formula *zi an-na zi ki-a* 'by the life of heaven and the life of earth' (see central entry `zi-an-na-zi-ki-a-nish-ilim-oath-by-life-of-heaven-and-earth-cross-corpus` for the full Sumerian–Akkadian–Hebrew oath-formula cluster). The verb *pad3* 'to find / to invoke (in oath)' is the standard Sumerian oath-cutting verb. The full dual-form oath-formula and the cross-corpus comparanda (Akkadian *nīš šamê u erṣetim*; Hebrew *chai YHWH*; Matt 5:34-37 reception-history) are documented at the central entry; this single-form deployment is the abbreviated invocation.

i18n.en: He lay with her in the marsh; he lay with her in the marsh, in joy.
Enki had his semen poured for Damgalnuna.

lines.commentary: *Damgalnuna* (literally 'great spouse of the princely-one (*Nun* = Enki)') is the consort of Enki under one of her several names. The next line (73) names the recipient of the semen as *Ninhursag*; the immediate juxtaposition equates the two — Damgalnuna and Ninhursag are the same goddess under different epithets (see central entry `nintur-nintud-ninhursaga-birth-goddess-epithet-cluster-cross-corpus` for the multi-epithet birth-goddess cluster; the overlay entry `damgalnuna-ninhursag-equation-sumerian` documents the per-composition Damgalnuna identification).

i18n.en: Ninhursag took the semen into her womb, the semen of Enki.
She received the semen into her womb, the semen of Enki.
One day was for her one month.

lines.commentary: Lines 75-83 (and the parallel sequences at 102-104, 122-123) deploy the **nine-day divine pregnancy** formula: 'one day was for her one month ... nine days were for her nine months, the months of womanhood'. The one-day-equals-one-month telescoping accelerates the ordinary nine-month human gestation into nine days of divine time, signaling the divinity of the mother (Ninhursag, then her daughter Ninnisig, then Ninkura) and the divinity of the offspring. The formula recurs three times in this composition (each generational pregnancy in the Enki-fathered line). See overlay entry `nine-day-divine-pregnancy-formula-sumerian` for the cross-corpus comparative-mythology context (Atrahasis I.iv parallel; Akkadian *birth-of-the-divine-child* formulae).

i18n.en: Two days were for her two months.
Three days were for her three months.
Four days were for her four months.
Five days were for her five months.
Six days were for her six months.
[Seven] days were for her seven months.
[Eight] days were for her eight <months>.
[Nine] days were for her nine months, the months of womanhood.
Like [fine oil, like] fine oil, like the oil of abundance,
[Nintur,] the mother of the Land,
[like fine oil] —
gave birth to [Ninnisig].
Ninnisig went out at the bank of the watercourse.
Enki was hanging out in the marsh, he was hanging out there;
to his minister Isimud he spoke:

lines.commentary: *Isimud* (the two-faced messenger-god) is Enki's *sukkal* — the chamberlain-vizier office of Mesopotamian divine and royal courts. Isimud is the standard divine *sukkal* of Enki across the Sumerian Enki-narrative corpus (Enki and the World Order; Inana and Enki; Adapa-tradition predecessors); his iconography in cylinder-seal art shows him facing both forwards and backwards. The Sumerian *sukkal* (loaned into Akkadian as *sukkallu*) is the technical office of intermediary between a high-ranking person (here a god) and his interlocutors. See overlay entry `isimud-vizier-of-enki-sumerian` for Isimud's cross-corpus appearances.

i18n.en: 'Shall I not kiss this fair young one?'
'Shall I not kiss the fair Ninnisig?'
His minister Isimud answered him:
'Shall you not kiss this fair young one?'
'Shall you not <kiss> the fair Ninnisig?'
'My king will sail there — let me steer; he will sail there — let me steer!'
He set one foot in the boat;
the other he set on dry land.
He pressed her to the breast; he kissed her.
Enki had his semen poured into her womb.
She received the semen into her womb, the semen of Enki.
One day was for her one month.
Two days were for her two months.
Nine days were for her nine months, the months of womanhood.
Like fine [oil, like] fine oil, like the oil of abundance,
[Ninnisig], like fine <oil>, like fine oil, like the oil of abundance —
gave birth to Nin[kura].
Ninkura [went out at the bank of the watercourse].
Enki was hanging out in the marsh, [he was hanging out there];
to his minister Isimud [he spoke]:
'Shall I not [kiss] this fair young one?'
'Shall I not kiss the fair Ninkura?'
His minister Isimud answered him:
'Kiss for him this fair young one!'
'Kiss for him the fair Ninkura!'
'My king will sail there — let me steer; he will sail there — let me steer!'
He set one foot in the boat;
the other he set on dry land.
He pressed her to the breast; he kissed her.
Enki had his semen poured into her womb.
She received the semen into her womb, the semen of Enki.
One day was for her one month.
Nine days were for her nine months, the months of womanhood, [for her].
Like fine oil, like fine oil, like the oil [of abundance],
Ninkura, like fine <oil>, like fine oil, like the oil of abundance —
gave birth to Uttu, the flourishing woman.
Nintur spoke to Uttu:
'Let me give you advice — take my advice [in hand].'
'Let me speak a word — [give your ear to my word].'
'There is a single man in the marsh — he is hanging out, [he is hanging out>].'
'Enki [is hanging out in the marsh, he is hanging out>].'
[9 lines fragmentary.]
[9 lines fragmentary.] '... ...'
'[... Uttu], the flourishing woman, ... ...'

lines.translit: […] X X X A NA X […]

i18n.en: '... your heart ...'
'[Bring cucumbers in their] dripping vessels!'

lines.commentary: Lines 147-176 narrate Enki's seduction of Uttu (his great-granddaughter), conducted by impersonating a gardener bearing three plant-gifts: *ukuš2* 'cucumber', *^ĝišḫašḫur* 'apple-tree fruit', and *^ĝišĝeštin* 'grape / wine'. The garden-produce-as-seduction-vehicle is a recurring Sumerian narrative motif (cf. Inana and Šukaletuda; the Dumuzi-and-Inana courtship-corpus); the lexemes name **horticultural products** of Mesopotamian-Gulf orchard-agriculture, not specifically-symbolic species. The cross-corpus comparison with **Gen 3** *peri ets ha-da'at tov va-ra* 'fruit of the tree of knowing good and bad' is structural-and-thematic — both narratives deploy a **garden-fruit-and-disobedience-or-disruption** pattern — but the parallel is **not etymological-identification** of the cucumber / apple / grape with the Genesis forbidden-fruit (the Hebrew text does not name the fruit; medieval Latin tradition's *malum / pomum* 'apple' is a vernacular substitution). Named scholarship: Alster *Dilmun, the Cradle of Civilization* 1983; Black *et al.* *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* 2004; Westermann *Genesis 1-11* BKAT on the comparative-mythology; Wenham *Genesis 1-15* WBC 1987. See overlay entry `cucumber-apple-grape-garden-gift-seduction-sumerian-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: 'Bring apples in their swelling [bunches]!'
'Bring grapes in their bunches!'
'In the house may you take my tethering rope!'
'Enki, may you take my tethering rope!'
A second time, while he filled it with water,
he filled the embankment with water.
He filled the canals with water.
He filled the fallow ground with water.
The gardener, in his joy from the dust, [...]
he embraced him, neck against neck.
'Who are you, ... the orchard ...?'
Enki [says to] the gardener: '[...]'
[4 lines missing.]
[4 lines missing.] '[He brought cucumbers in their] dripping [vessels];'
'he brought apples in their swelling bunches;'
'he brought grapes in their bunches and filled his lap.'
Enki made his eyes flash green; he took up the sceptre in his hand.
Enki set his foot to Uttu's;
he struck at her house — 'Open up! Open up!'
'Who are you?'
'I am the gardener — let me give you cucumber, apple, [and grape] as your due.'
Uttu, in the joy of her heart, opened up the house for him.
Enki — to Uttu the flourishing woman —
gave her cucumbers in their dripping vessels;
gave her apples in their swelling bunches;
gave her grapes in their bunches.
He [poured] beer into the great drinking-vessel.

lines.translit: ^duttu munus NI-buluĝ3 gabu2 mu-na-ab-sig10-ge šu mu-na-sag3-ge

i18n.en: Uttu the flourishing woman placed (him) on her left and beat on his hand.
Enki — for Uttu — swelled himself with joy.
He took her by the breast — she lay in his lap.
He stroked her thigh; he stroked her with his hand.
He took her by the breast — she lay in his lap.
He stiffened against the youngling; he kissed her.
Enki poured semen into Uttu's womb.
She received the semen into her womb, the semen of Enki.

lines.translit: ^duttu munus sag9-ga a2^? ḫaš2-ĝu10 im-me a2^? bar-ĝu10 a2^? ša3^?-ba-ĝu10 im-[me]

i18n.en: Uttu, the fair woman, cried: 'Woe — my thighs!' she said. 'Woe my outsides! Woe my insides!' she [said].
Ninhursag wiped the semen from the thighs.

lines.commentary: Ninhursag intervenes after Enki's transgression against Uttu. The wiping of the semen prepares for the eight-plants sequence at lines 190-197: from the wiped-semen the eight plants are conjectured to spring (the lacuna at 188-189 obscures the connecting narrative, but the Black *et al.* reconstruction follows Kramer 1944 in supplying the seed-becomes-plants link). Ninhursag is here named under her *Ninhursag* epithet; see central entry `nintur-nintud-ninhursaga-birth-goddess-epithet-cluster-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: [2 lines fragmentary.]
[2 lines fragmentary.] [The tree-plant grew up].
[The honey-plant grew up].
[The sar-plant grew up].
[The esparto-grass grew up].
[The atutu-plant grew up].
[The astaltal-plant] grew up.
[The ...-plant] grew up.
[The amharu-plant] grew up.
Enki was hanging out in the marsh; he was hanging out there.
To his minister Isimud he spoke:
'These plants — I would decree their destiny.'

lines.commentary:
Lines 190-219 cluster the **eight plants** that Enki sees, asks Isimud to identify, and eats. The plants are: *u2-ĝiš* (tree-plant), *u2-lal3* (honey-plant), *u2-sar-ra* (sar-plant), *^u2A.NUMUN2* (esparto-grass), *^u2a-tu-tu* (atutu-plant), *^u2aš-tal2-tal2* (astaltal-plant), an eighth plant whose name is lost in lacuna, and *^u2am-ḫa-ru* (amharu-plant). Six of the eight have no securely-identified botanical referent (lexica gloss them only as 'type of plant'); only *u2-lal3* (honey-plant) and *^u2A.NUMUN2* (esparto) have referents fixed by lexical-list comparison.

The Sumerian *nam tar* 'to decree a destiny' idiom (see central entry `nam-sumerian-destiny-fate-cross-corpus`) signals an act of cosmic-categorization: Enki proposes to determine the plants' destinies — that is, to assign their roles in the world's order. The narrative reverses this: instead of decreeing their destinies, he eats them and falls ill. The transgression triggers the chapter's central crisis and motivates Ninhursag's curse (220-221).

Cross-corpus comparative-mythology: the **eight plants Enki eats** structurally parallel **Gen 2:17 / 3:6** *etz ha-da'at tov va-ra* — the forbidden-tree whose fruit Eve and Adam eat — in the **forbidden-or-improper-food-causing-illness-or-transformation** typology. The parallel is structural (eating-the-forbidden-thing leads to a body-altering consequence) rather than etymological-or-genealogical. In the Sumerian narrative, the divine actor (Enki) is the eater; in the Hebrew, the human is the eater. In the Sumerian, the eaten produces illness localized to body-parts; in the Hebrew, the eaten opens *yedi'ah* 'knowing'. Named scholarship: Kramer 1944 *BASOR* 96; Alster 'Enki and Ninhursag' *Acta Sumerologica* 1978; Black *et al.* 2004; Hallo *Origins* 1996; Wenham *Genesis 1-15* WBC 1987; Westermann *Genesis 1-11* BKAT. See overlay entry `eight-plants-enki-eats-forbidden-food-motif`.

i18n.en: 'What is this one? What is this one?'
His minister Isimud answered him:
'My [king], it is the tree-plant,' he says.
He cut it down for him; he ate [it].
'My king, it is the honey-plant,' he says.
He tore it out for him; he ate it.
'My king, it is the sar-plant,' he <says>.
He cut it down for him; he <ate it>.
'My king, it is the esparto-grass,' he <says>.
He tore it out for him; he <ate it>.
'[My king], it is the atutu-plant,' he <says>.
[He cut it down for him]; he <ate it>.
'[My king, it is the astaltal]-plant,' he <says>.
[He tore it out for him; he ate it].
'[My king, it is the ...-plant,' he says].
[He cut it down for him]; he <ate it>.
'[My king, it is the] amharu-plant,' he says.
[He tore it] out; he ate it.
[Enki] decreed the destiny of the plants; he knew them in their heart.
Ninhursag swore an oath in the name of Enki:

lines.commentary: *nam-erim2 kud* is the technical Sumerian idiom for **cutting / decreeing the curse-oath** — the formal-juridical oath whose violation triggers self-cursing on the swearer. The cognate Akkadian *māmītu* / *māmīta nadû* (literally 'to throw / cast the oath-curse') is the Akkadian-language form attested across the Old Babylonian and Standard Babylonian corpus, with the noun *māmītu* identifying the binding-curse that holds the oath in force. Ninhursag's *nam-erim2* here is the most severe oath-form available to her — a curse-oath, not a simple assertory oath. Named scholarship: Lambert 'Three Unpublished Fragments of the Tukulti-Ninurta Epic' *AfO* 1957; CAD M/1 189-195 *māmītu*. See overlay entry `nam-erim-curse-oath-cutting-formula-sumerian`.

lines.translit: i-bi2 na-aĝ2-til3-la en-na ba-ug5-ge-a i-bi2 ba-ra-an-bar-re-en

i18n.en: 'Until he is dead I shall not look upon him with the eye of life.'

lines.commentary: The *i-bi2 nam-til3-la* — 'eye of life' (literally 'eye of the life-state', with *nam-til3* the abstract-substantive of *til3* 'to live') — is the famous Sumerian idiom for the **life-giving / paradisal-restorative gaze**. The Sumerian *til3* is paired-and-contrasted with *zi* (covered by central entry `zi-sumerian-breath-of-life-cross-corpus`) in the corpus's life-vocabulary; both designate aspects of vital-existence (*til3* the durative-state of being-alive; *zi* the breath / animating-principle). Ninhursag's withholding the *eye of life* condemns Enki to die from the eight-plant-eating illness until she chooses to restore him. The expression's parallel-with-its-inverse — the **withering gaze** of divinity — is widely-attested in Mesopotamian incantation and ritual texts. See overlay entry `eye-of-life-sumerian-paradisal-gaze-idiom`.

i18n.en: The Anuna sat down in the dust.
The fox spoke to Enlil:

lines.commentary: The **fox** (*ka5-a*) appears here as a divine-court mediator-figure, negotiating with Enlil for a reward in exchange for retrieving Ninhursag. The Sumerian fox-as-trickster-mediator is attested across the Sumerian literary tradition — the ETCSL animal-fable corpus (5.9.x) preserves the fox in proverbial and fable-narrative contexts; the fox's role in this composition follows the trickster-mediator type, brokering between divine parties for negotiated compensation. The fox's identity as a divine or quasi-divine actor (rather than a literal animal) is the standard scholarly reading. Named scholarship: Alster 'Enki and Ninhursag' *Acta Sumerologica* 1978 on the fox-mediator function; Black *et al.* 2004; Vanstiphout 'The Old Babylonian Literary Catalogue' *Aula Orientalis* 1986 on the fox-fable tradition. See overlay entry `fox-mediator-sumerian-mythological-figure`.

i18n.en: 'If I bring Ninhursag to you, what shall be my gift?'
Enlil answered the fox:
'If you bring Ninhursag (back),'
'in my city I will plant two birch-trees for you — your name shall be uttered.'
The fox anointed his body once;
he combed his hair once;
he applied kohl to his eye once.
[4 lines fragmentary.]
[4 lines fragmentary.] '[To Nibru I will] go — Enlil [...].'
'To [Urim] I will go — Nanna [...].'
'To [Larsam] I will go — Utu [...].'
'To [Unug] I will go — Inana ...'
'... so it was — my life carry away ...'
Ninhursag ...
[3 lines fragmentary.]
[3 lines fragmentary.] '... NE ...'
'... BA NE DU'
Ninhursag came running to the house.
The Anuna seized her garment.

lines.commentary: The **garment-seizure** is a stock formal-detention gesture in ANE legal-and-narrative texts: grasping the hem or fringe of a garment constitutes a juridical act of detention, supplication, or claim-establishment. The same gesture recurs in Akkadian *qarābu sissikta* 'to seize the hem (in supplication)' and in Hebrew narrative (1 Sam 15:27 — Samuel seizes the hem of Saul's robe; Hag 2:12 — the hem-of-garment carries-or-fails-to-carry holiness). Here the Anuna restrain Ninhursag (who has come running from her place of retreat) to ensure she remains for the healing-deity births. Named scholarship: M. Malul 'Studies in Mesopotamian Legal Symbolism' AOAT 221, 1988 on the hem-grasping legal-act; M. Greenberg *Ezekiel 1-20* AB 1983 on the Hebrew hem-grasping parallels. See overlay entry `garment-seizure-formal-detention-ane`.

i18n.en: They made (a) LI ...
They decreed a destiny.
They released the hand-(of) LI.
Ninhursag had Enki sit at her vulva.

lines.commentary: Ninhursag places Enki at her *gal4* 'vulva' as the physical-and-ritual locus from which she will birth the eight healing-deities (lines 254-271). The body-from-body birth-locus framing makes the eight-deity sequence into a single divine-self-multiplication act: each body-part of Enki becomes a deity through Ninhursag's body. See central entry `nintur-nintud-ninhursaga-birth-goddess-epithet-cluster-cross-corpus` and overlay entry `eight-healing-deities-birth-by-body-part-sequence`.

i18n.en: '... hand ... outside ...'
'My brother — what part of you hurts you?'
'The top of my head hurts me.'
She gave birth to Ab-u out (of it).

lines.commentary:
Lines 254-271 are the **eight healing-deities birth-by-body-part** sequence — the chapter's signature structural figure. Ninhursag, having had Enki placed at her vulva (252), repeatedly asks Enki to name the body-part that hurts, and from each pained body-part births a healing-deity whose name encodes the body-part. The formulaic structure is *šeš-ĝu10 a-na-zu a-ra-gig X-ĝu10 ma-gig* 'My brother, what part of you hurts you? My X hurts me' followed by *Y im-ma-ra-an-tu-ud* 'she bore Y out (of it)'.

The eight pairings are: (1) *ugu-dilim2* 'top of head' → **Ab-u** (256); (2) *pa siki* 'lock of hair' → **Ninsikila** (259); (3) *giri17* 'nose' → **Ningiriutud** (261); (4) *ka* 'mouth' → **Ninkasi** (263); (5) *zi* 'throat / breath' → **Nazi / Nanše** (265); (6) *a2* 'arm' → **Azimua** (267); (7) *ti* 'rib' → **Ninti** (269); (8) *zag* 'side' → **Ensag** (271). In two of the eight cases — Nazi and Ninti — the **philological pun** is the diagnostic structural figure: the body-part lexeme is **homophonous with a life-vocabulary lexeme** in Sumerian. *zi* 'throat' is homophonous with *zi* 'breath / life'; *ti* 'rib' is homophonous with *til3* 'to live'. The two pun-deities are paired at lines 265 (Nazi) and 269 (Ninti) — the structural-parallel argues for reading the *^dna-zi* of 265 as *Nazi* preserving the pun (see line 265 commentary and overlay entry `nazi-nanse-throat-life-sumerian-philological-pun`).

Named scholarship: Kramer 1944 *BASOR* 96 (the foundational analysis of the eight healing-deities); Kramer 1963 *The Sumerians*; Alster 'Enki and Ninhursag' *Acta Sumerologica* 1978; Jacobsen *The Harps that Once* 1987; Black *et al.* *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* 2004; on the Mesopotamian body-part-and-healing-deity associations more broadly: M. Stol *Birth in Babylonia and the Bible* CM 14, 2000; M. Geller *Ancient Babylonian Medicine* 2010. See overlay entry `eight-healing-deities-birth-by-body-part-sequence`.

i18n.en: 'My brother — what part of you hurts you?'
'The locks of my hair hurt me.'
She gave birth to Ninsikila out (of it).
'My brother — what part of you hurts you? My nose hurts me.'
She gave birth to Ningiriutud out (of it).
'My brother — what part of you hurts you? My mouth hurts me.'
She gave birth to Ninkasi out [(of it)].

lines.commentary: **Ninkasi** is the Sumerian beer-and-brewing goddess. Her name encodes *ka* 'mouth' (the body-part that hurts Enki at 262) plus *si* 'to fill'; her destiny-assignment at line 276 *niĝ2 šag4 si ḫe2-a* 'let her be that which fills the heart / belly' is a pun-of-function alluding to her beer-pouring role (Sumerian *šag4* 'heart / belly' is the canonical Sumerian belly-as-vessel-of-feeling-and-drink). The cross-corpus text *Hymn to Ninkasi* (ETCSL 4.23.1; OB Sumerian beer-hymn with full brewing-recipe) is the principal Sumerian Ninkasi-source; her presence in this composition as the **mouth-healer** is the diagnostic-Mesopotamian deification of mouth-pleasure / nourishment. Named scholarship: M. Civil 'A Hymn to the Beer Goddess and a Drinking Song' in *Studies Presented to A. Leo Oppenheim* 1964; M. W. Stol 'Beer in Neo-Babylonian Times' in *Drinking in Ancient Societies* 1994; Black *et al.* 2004; on cross-corpus brewing-vocabulary: P. Damerow *Sumerian Beer* CDLJ 2012. See central entry `ninkasi-beer-brewing-goddess-sumerian-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: 'My brother — what part of you hurts you? My throat hurts me.'
She gave birth to Nazi (alternate manuscript: Nanše) out [(of it)].

lines.commentary: The cuneiform writing *^dna-zi* admits two scholarly readings. **Nazi** (Kramer 1944 *BASOR* 96 'Dilmun, the Land of the Living'; followed by Jacobsen *The Harps that Once*; Black *et al.* *The Literature of Ancient Sumer*) preserves the **structural-pun** with the preceding line 264 *zi-ĝu10 ma-gig* 'my throat (= *zi*) hurts me'. Sumerian *zi* spans both 'throat / windpipe' and 'breath / life'; the deity born from Enki's pained throat-and-breath is *Nazi*, 'the (lady) of life-breath'. The structural-parallel to the line 268-269 *ti*/*til3* pun at Nin-ti (where *ti* 'rib' is homophonous with *til3* 'to live') is the philological argument: the composition pairs two **body-part-life pun** birth-deities. **Nanše** (the ETCSL lemma; Falkenstein; Heimpel) reflects the later identification of the deity with the Lagash city-goddess Nanše. Both readings are defensible; this translation foregrounds *Nazi* per the structural-pun argument and notes the variant inline per the project's `manuscript-variant-inline-rendering-convention`. The cross-corpus details are in the overlay entry `nazi-nanse-throat-life-sumerian-philological-pun`.

i18n.en: 'My brother — what part of you hurts you? My arm hurts me.'
She gave birth to Azimua out [(of it)].
'My brother — what part of you hurts you? My rib [hurts me].'
She gave birth to Ninti out [(of it)].

lines.commentary:
**Ninti** is the central philological-pun of the chapter. The deity is born from Enki's pained *ti* 'rib' at line 268 (*ti-ĝu10 ma-gig* 'my rib hurts me'); her name *^dnin-ti* simultaneously reads as **'Lady of the rib'** (from *ti* 'rib') and **'Lady of life'** (from *til3* 'to live' — the verb is homophonous with the rib-noun in Sumerian, both written *ti* in this form). The two senses are not synonymous but co-resident in the single name; the composition exploits the homophony as the structural-organizing-principle of the eight-deity sequence (Ninti at line 269 pairs with Nazi at line 265 — both deploy the body-part / life-vocabulary pun).

**The cross-corpus comparative-mythology observation.** Kramer 1944 *BASOR* 96 'Dilmun, the Land of the Living' identified this Sumerian *ti*/*til3* pun as the **comparative-mythology precursor** to the Hebrew Gen 2:21-22 *tzela* 'rib / side' narrative and the Gen 3:20 *chavvah em kol-chai* 'Chavvah, mother of all the living' naming. The Hebrew narrative is structurally-parallel — a body-part-and-life-vocabulary pairing — but the Hebrew **lacks the pun**, because Hebrew *tzela* 'side / rib' is not homophonous with Hebrew *chai* 'life' or *chavvah* 'Chavvah'. Kramer's reading is that the Hebrew text **preserves the structural-motif** (a female life-giver derived from a male body-part) **without preserving the underlying Sumerian wordplay**, because the linguistic conditions for the pun do not obtain in Hebrew.

**Operational disavowals — paramount at this entry.** This comparative-mythology observation is **not an etymological-identity claim**: Sumerian and Hebrew belong to **unrelated language-families** (Sumerian is a language-isolate; Hebrew is Northwest Semitic), and no philological-cognation between Sumerian *ti*/*til3* and Hebrew *tzela* / *chai* is asserted. The comparison is at the level of **structural-mythological-motif** (the body-part-as-life-source narrative pattern); the Hebrew text is a **possible cultural-memory transformation** of the Mesopotamian motif, not a linguistic-cognate. The comparative scholarship is contested in detail; Kramer's strongest reading has been variously endorsed (Hallo *Origins* 1996; Sarna *Genesis* JPS 1989) and qualified (Westermann *Genesis 1-11* BKAT — accepts the motif-parallel, cautions against over-reading; Wenham *Genesis 1-15* WBC 1987 — cautious endorsement). This translation surfaces the observation under named scholarship and at no point imports a **Christian-Eve-typology pre-resolution** (Pauline / Marian / Augustinian readings of Eve are outside the scope of this comparative-philological note) or any project-specific re-framing of Eve as 'Sumerian-borrowed', 'engineered female', or otherwise.

Named scholarship: Kramer 1944 *BASOR* 96; Kramer 1963 *The Sumerians*; Hallo *Origins of the Ancient Near Eastern Religious Traditions* 1996; Sarna *Genesis* JPS Commentary 1989; Wenham *Genesis 1-15* WBC 1987; Westermann *Genesis 1-11* BKAT; Heidel *The Babylonian Genesis* 2nd ed. 1951; Cassuto *From Adam to Noah* 1961; Black *et al.* *The Literature of Ancient Sumer* 2004. For the Hebrew side, see central entries `tzela-side` (Gen 2:21-22 *tzela*) and `chavvah-em-kol-chai` (Gen 3:20 naming). For the Sumerian *zi* throat/life-breath pun-parallel at Nazi, see line 265 commentary and overlay entry `nazi-nanse-throat-life-sumerian-philological-pun`. The full cross-corpus comparative-mythology bibliography is at central entry `nin-ti-lady-of-rib-lady-of-life-eve-sumerian-philological-pun-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: 'My brother — what part of you hurts you? My side [hurts me].'
She gave birth to Ensag out [(of it)].
'For these little ones — for whom you have been given birth — let there be a gift, an obligation.'
'Let Ab-u be the lord of the plant.'
'Let Ninsikila be the lord of Magan.'

lines.commentary: **Magan** (*ma2-gan-na*) is the ANE toponym for the Oman peninsula / eastern-Arabian coast (Potts *The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity* 1990 vol. 1; Heimpel 'Das untere Meer' *ZA* 77 1987; Glassner 'Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha' in *The Indian Ocean in Antiquity* 1996). The Magan-trade-network ran copper, diorite stone, and finished goods between Oman and the Mesopotamian heartland from the late third millennium. Ninsikila's destiny-assignment to Magan paired with Ensag's to Dilmun at line 280 situates the closing in the SE-Mesopotamian Gulf trade-geography. See overlay entry `magan-toponym-ane-trade-geography`.

i18n.en: 'Let Ningiriutud marry Ninazu.'
'Let Ninkasi be that which fills the heart.'
'Let Nazi (alternate manuscript: Nanše) marry Nindara.'

lines.commentary: The deity birthed at line 265 receives her destiny here. The Nindara-marriage assignment is the conventional pairing of Nanše-the-Lagash-goddess with Nindara (her consort in the Lagash cult-tradition), which is one of the data points for reading *^dna-zi* here as Nanše rather than Nazi. The same surface-rendering convention as line 265 applies; see the overlay entry `nazi-nanse-throat-life-sumerian-philological-pun`.

i18n.en: 'Let Azi[mua] marry [Nin]gišzida.'

lines.commentary: **Ningišzida** ('Lord of the steadfast tree') is the Sumerian chthonic-vegetation deity, paired with Dumuzi as gatekeeper of An's heaven in *Adapa* and elsewhere; his iconography in third- and second-millennium glyptic shows him as a horned-serpent or as a deity flanked by horned-serpents. His marriage to Azimua here pairs Enki's *arm*-healing-deity (born from *a2* 'arm' at 267) with the chthonic-vegetation deity, completing the Magan-Dilmun-Sumer geography of the closing destinies. Named scholarship: F. Wiggermann *RlA* 9 368-373 *Nin-ĝiš-zida*; Jacobsen *Treasures of Darkness* 1976; Black *et al.* 2004. See overlay entry `ninĝišzida-chthonic-vegetation-deity-sumerian`.

i18n.en: 'Let Nin[ti] be the lady of the month.'

lines.commentary: Ninti's destiny-assignment as **lady of the month** is a calendrical-domain office (the Sumerian *itid* 'month' is the lunar-period of the Mesopotamian month-calendar). The assignment carries the *ti* / *til3* pun forward: in the gestation-formula at lines 75-83 the *months of womanhood* (*itid nam-munus-a*) frame the divine pregnancy, so Ninti-as-lady-of-the-month is structurally the patron of the **monthly cycle that sustains life** — preserving the rib/life pun in her destiny-office. See central entry `nin-ti-lady-of-rib-lady-of-life-eve-sumerian-philological-pun-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: 'Let [Ensa]g be the lord of Dilmun.'

lines.commentary: **Ensag** (the *side*-healing-deity born at line 271 from *zag* 'side') receives the closing destiny-office: lordship over Dilmun. The composition thereby closes by returning to the opening Dilmun-paradise frame (lines 1-10) — the paradise that began as ungoverned-pure-land receives a tutelary lord, and the cosmographic-circle is closed. The Ensag-Dilmun and Ninsikila-Magan paired destinies (Ninsikila is the original Dilmun-deity invoked at 9) reorganize the Gulf-trade-cosmography into Ensag-Dilmun and Ninsikila-Magan. See central entry `dilmun-eastern-paradise-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: [Enki] — praise!
